per_claim.claim: William Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet.

judgments.passage_text: Romeo and Juliet is a tragedy written by William Shakespeare early in his career about two young Italian star-crossed lovers whose deaths ultimately reconcile their feuding families. It was among Shakespeare's most popular plays during his lifetime and, along with Hamlet, is one of his most frequently performed plays. Shakespeare is believed to have written the play between 1594 and 1596. The earliest surviving printed version, the First Quarto (Q1), was published in 1597. The story is based on an Italian tale translated into verse as The Tragicall Historye of Romeus and Juliet by Arthur Brooke in 1562.

His plays have been translated into every major language and are performed more often than those of any other playwright.

per_claim.claim: The speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second.

judgments.passage_text: The speed of light in vacuum, commonly denoted c, is a universal physical constant equal to exactly 299,792,458 metres per second (approximately 300,000 km/s or 186,000 mi/s). According to the special theory of relativity, c is the upper limit for the speed at which conventional matter, energy, or any signal carrying information can travel through space. In 1983, the metre was redefined in the International System of Units (SI) as the distance travelled by light in vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second, making the speed of light in vacuum exact by definition.
judgments.evidence: The speed of light in vacuum, commonly denoted c, is a universal physical constant equal to exactly 299,792,458 metres per second

judgments.passage_text: The metre is the fundamental unit of length in the International System of Units (SI). Since 1983, the metre has been defined as the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of exactly 1/299,792,458 of a second. This definition fixes the speed of light to exactly 299,792,458 metres per second. Previously, the metre had been defined in terms of a physical artefact—a platinum-iridium bar kept at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Sèvres, France.

Later on, many successive dynasties built and maintained multiple stretches of border walls. The most well-known sections of the wall were built by the Ming dynasty (1368–1644). Charles Darwin popularised the term 'natural selection' contrasting it with artificial selection. The concept was independently conceived by Darwin and Wallace. Natural selection acts on the phenotype, the characteristics of the organism which actually interact with the environment, but the genetic (heritable) basis of any phenotype that gives that phenotype a reproductive advantage will become more common in a population.

per_claim.claim: The fall of the Western Roman Empire resulted from multiple interconnected factors rather than a single cause.

judgments.passage_title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
judgments.passage_text: The fall of the Western Roman Empire was the process of decline in the Western Roman Empire in which it failed to enforce its rule. The date most often cited for the 'fall' is 476 AD, when Romulus Augustulus, the last emperor of the Western Roman Empire, was deposed by the Germanic chieftain Odoacer. Historians have proposed numerous theories including military overextension, the debasement of currency, political instability, overreliance on slave labor, and the increasing pressure from barbarian invasions from both Germanic tribes and the Huns.
judgments.evidence: Historians have proposed numerous theories including military overextension, the debasement of currency, political instability, overreliance on slave labor, and the increasing pressure from barbaria
judgments.reason: The evidence explicitly lists multiple factors (military overextension, currency debasement, political instability, overreliance on slave labor, and barbarian pressure) proposed by historians, directly supporting the claim that the fall resulted from multiple interconnected factors rather than a single cause.

judgments.passage_text: The Migration Period, also known as the Barbarian Invasions, was a period during the decline of the Roman Empire around 300–700 AD in which there were widespread migrations of peoples, including the Huns, Goths, Vandals, and Franks into Western and Southern Europe. This era is often marked as the transition from Late Antiquity to the Early Middle Ages. The Migration Period was both a cause and effect of the instability of the Western Roman Empire, and it reshaped the ethnic and political landscape of Europe.

judgments.reason: L'evidenza menziona solo il periodo delle migrazioni come causa/effetto interconnesso, suggerendo una complessità ma non stabilisce esplicitamente che siano intervenuti molteplici fattori interconnessi come indicato nel claim.
